page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.u1-c1m2.3xlarge is a general-purpose virtual machine built on KVM virtualization and powered by an Intel Xeon x86_64 processor operating at 2.5 GHz. It provides 12 vCPUs distributed across 6 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading enabled. The CPU cache architecture includes 32 KB L1 data cache per core, 1.0 MB L2 cache per core, and a shared 33 MB L3 cache. Instruction set extensions include AVX, AVX-512F, AES, BMI2, ADX, and FMA, supporting accelerated mathematical operations and encryption. The system is provisioned with 24.0 GB of system memory, establishing a 1:2 vCPU-to-memory ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU.

The instance has no included local storage, requiring network-attached storage for persistent filesystems, and lacks dedicated GPU accelerators. Baseline network throughput is rated at 4 Gbps, and no complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned. Across standard computational benchmarks, the hardware demonstrates mid-tier capabilities. It recorded a Geekbench multi-core score of 6824.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 15004.59. Threaded file decompression via bzip3 reached 62.77 GB/sec, while static web serving throughput achieved 13.21 GB/sec.

Benchmark evaluation reveals distinct hardware characteristics, particularly regarding memory throughput. Cached small-block memory reads operate at 640.48 GB/sec, placed in the average tier. However, uncached large-block reads drop to 36.23 GB/sec, placing memory read bandwidth in the lower 25% of comparable cloud instances. This memory throughput bottleneck impacts larger compute profiles, as evidenced by medium 7B model LLM inference results of 23.95 tokens/sec during prompt processing and 8.1 tokens/sec during token generation.

With a 1:2 vCPU-to-memory allocation, ecs.u1-c1m2.3xlarge offers cost-effective CPU resource density for compute-centric, non-memory-heavy tasks. It is well-fitted for static web serving, containerized application logic, background build tasks, and moderate caching tiers such as Redis, where it achieved 11.69 million SET operations per second. It is less suitable for large in-memory databases, dense local I/O workloads, or deep learning inference demanding high sustained memory bandwidth.
